name: Ahlai
title: Daughter of Shelem from the Jerahmeelite branch of the tribe of Judah
summary: Ahlai appears in two different contexts in 1 Chronicles. In the genealogy of the Jerahmeelite branch of the tribe of Judah, Ahlai is mentioned as the daughter of Sheshan (1 Chron 2:31). Since Sheshan had no sons, he gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha as a wife, and through this marriage the family line was continued via their son Attai (1 Chron 2:34–35). In the list of David’s mighty warriors, Zabad is also referred to as "son of Ahlai" (1 Chron 11:41). Whether these two occurrences of the name refer to the same person or to two different individuals remains an unresolved question. If it concerns one person, then "son of" in 1 Chron 11:41 must be understood in a broad sense as "descendant of," since according to the genealogy Zabad is several generations removed from Ahlai. Ahlai’s place in family history sheds light on inheritance practices of that time and shows how people of non-Israelite origin could be incorporated into Israel’s tribal community through marriage.
roles: link in the continuation of Shelem's family line

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Judah
keyEvents.description: Ahlai is mentioned as the daughter of Shelem in the genealogy of the Jerahmeelite branch of the tribe of Judah. Since Shelem had no sons, he gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha as a wife so that his family line would continue. Their son was Attai.

keyEvents.title: Ancestor of Zabad, one of David's warriors
keyEvents.description: In the list of David's mighty men, Zabad is referred to as "son of Ahlai" (1 Chron 11:41). According to the genealogy in 1 Chron 2:36, Zabad is a later link in the family line after Attai and Nathan. It is debated whether this refers to the same Ahlai who was the daughter of Shelem or if these are two different people with the same name.

versions.summary: Ahlai is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles. The name appears twice in the genealogies: once as the daughter of Shelem from the tribe of Judah, and once as the father of Zabad, one of David's warriors. It is debated whether this refers to one or two different people.
versions.title: Descendant of Jerahmeel
versions.reason: [major] The title says 'Descendant of Jesrakel', but Ahlai is a descendant of Jerahmeel (through Sheshan), not 'Jesrakel'. Jesrakel is not a known biblical name in this context. It should be corrected to 'Jerahmeel'.; [major] The role 'warrior' is not correct for Ahlai. It is Zabad (son of Ahlai) who is mentioned as one of David's warriors. Ahlai himself is primarily known from genealogical records. If Ahlai is identified as the daughter of Sheshan, the role 'daughter' or simply 'person in the genealogy' would be more appropriate. The role should reflect that Ahlai is mainly known from genealogical lists.; [minor] The family relationships only reflect one identification of Ahlai (as father of Zabad from 1 Chr 11:41). If Ahlai in 1 Chr 2:31 is the same person (daughter of Sheshan), the spouse field should potentially include 'Jarha' (the Egyptian servant). Since it is debated whether there is one or two persons, this should be reflected better.; [minor] Verse 42 in 1 Chr 11 concerns another warrior (Adina, son of Shiza), not Zabad. It should be limited to verse 41.; [minor] The summary is generally good but could be improved by explicitly mentioning the connection to the Jerahmeel lineage and providing a bit more context about its genealogical significance.; [minor] There are no footnotes that could shed light on the interesting question of whether Ahlai is one or two persons, the meaning of the name, and the unusual practice of giving a daughter to an Egyptian servant.

versions.summary: Ahlai is a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles. The name appears twice in the genealogies: once as the daughter of Sheban from the Jerahmeelite branch of the tribe of Judah (1 Chron 2:31), and once as the father of Zabad, one of David's warriors (1 Chron 11:41). It is debated whether these refer to one or two different individuals. Sheban had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha to preserve the family line. Through this union, the lineage continued.
versions.title: Descendant of Jerahmeel from the tribe of Judah
versions.reason: [major] According to 1 Chr 2:34-35, Sheshan gave his daughter (Ahlai) in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha. Spouse should therefore be set to 'jarha'.; [minor] The second keyEvent ('Genealogy through Jarha') largely overlaps with the first ('Mentioned in Judah's genealogy'). They use almost the same verses and describe the same event. Consider merging them to avoid repetition.; [minor] The role 'daughter of Sheshan' is more a family relationship than a role. Since the text also mentions that Ahlai may be the father of Zabad (one of David's warriors), the roles could better reflect both identifications in the text.; [minor] The summary is good, but it closely resembles version 1. It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish itself from the earlier version and provide a more independent presentation.; [minor] The time period 'united-kingdom' is reasonable given the connection to David's warriors (1 Chr 11:41), though the genealogies may extend further back. Retained as acceptable.

versions.summary: Ahlai is known from two references in 1 Chronicles. In the genealogy of the Jerahmeel branch of the tribe of Judah, Ahlai is identified as the daughter of Sheshan (1 Chron 2:31). Because Sheshan had no sons, he gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha as a wife, and through this marriage the family line continued (1 Chron 2:34–35). In another context, Ahlai is mentioned as the father of Zabad, one of David's foremost warriors (1 Chron 11:41). The question of whether these two references concern one and the same person or two different individuals with the same name remains debated. Ahlai's place in the genealogy sheds light on both the inheritance practices of that time and the flexibility that existed for incorporating people of other ethnic backgrounds into Israel's tribal structure.
versions.title: Descendant of Jerahmeel and daughter of Sheban from the tribe of Judah
versions.reason: [major] In 1 Chr 2:35, Attai (not Zabad) is the child of Jarha and Sheshan's daughter. Zabad is a later descendant in this lineage (1 Chr 2:36). If we identify Ahlai with Sheshan's daughter, then the child should be Attai. Zabad is mentioned as 'son of Ahlai' in 1 Chr 11:41, but this could mean descendant rather than direct son.; [minor] Verse 36 in 1 Chr 2 concerns Attai as father of Natan, not directly about Ahlai. It may be included for context, but it is more precise to limit the reference to verses 31 and 34–35.; [minor] The title 'Father of Zabad among David's warriors' is imprecise because Ahlai in 1 Chr 2:31 is identified as female (daughter). If this is the same person, the title should reflect the uncertainty. If it is a different person, that too should be better reflected.; [minor] The time period 'united-kingdom' can be debated. Ahlai is mentioned in genealogies extending back before the united kingdom, but the connection to David (around 1000 BC) makes united-kingdom reasonable. Still, the person may have lived somewhat earlier.; [minor] The role 'matriarch in the Jerahmeel clan' is slightly imprecise – Ahlai is not the matriarch of the entire clan, but rather a link in continuing Sheshan's lineage within the Jerahmeel clan.

footnotes.text: The name Ahlai (אַחְלַי) may mean "Oh, if only!" or "would that" in Hebrew. It could be an expression of longing or a wishful exclamation, possibly reflecting the parents' hopes or circumstances at the child's birth.

That Sheban gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha as a wife was a highly unusual practice in Israelite culture. This arrangement ensured that the family line and inheritance would continue through the daughter, since Sheban had no male heirs. It illustrates remarkable flexibility in the marriage and inheritance customs of that time.

Biblical scholars debate whether Ahlai in 1 Chron 2:31 (daughter of Sheban) and Ahlai in 1 Chron 11:41 (father of Zabad) refer to the same person or two different individuals. Some scholars have suggested that "son of Ahlai" in 1 Chron 11:41 actually means "descendant of Ahlai," which could reconcile the two references.

The Jerahmeelites, to whom Ahlai belonged, were an important clan in the southern territory of Judah, in the Negev region. David had contact with them during his time as a fugitive and sent them portions of war spoils (1 Sam 27:10; 30:29). This connection may explain why a descendant of the Jerahmeelite clan later served among David's elite warriors.

The inclusion of Jarha, an Egyptian servant, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah is remarkable. It shows that non-Israelites could be integrated into the tribal system through marriage, and that ethnic background was not necessarily an absolute barrier to being included in God's people.

In 1 Chron 2:34–41 a complete lineage is given from Sheban through Jarha and his wife (Sheban's daughter) to Attai, and further through several generations down to Elishama. Zabad appears as the fourth link after Attai in this line (Attai – Nathan – Zabad). This suggests that "son of Ahlai" in 1 Chron 11:41 likely means "descendant of Ahlai" rather than a direct son.
